section.title: Preparations for the Temple
section.sectionRationale: Chapter 4 closed with kings from every nation traveling to hear Solomon's God-given wisdom. Chapter 5 shows that same wisdom at work in international diplomacy, as Hiram king of Tyre, long a friend of David, sends envoys to the new king. Solomon explains that David could not build a house for the Name of the LORD because of constant war, but now that the LORD has given him rest on every side, the time to build has come. Hiram gladly supplies cedar and cypress timber in exchange for food, the two kings seal a treaty, and Solomon conscripts a vast labor force to quarry stone and prepare timber, so that everything necessary is ready before a single stone of the temple itself is laid.
section.thesis: Because the LORD has given Solomon rest on every side, he is free to take up the house for the Name of the LORD that David was denied, and through a costly partnership of labor, timber, and stone with a Gentile king, Solomon prepares everything necessary before construction begins, so that even the temple's foundations testify to God's providence gathering the nations toward His house.
section.frameNote: Three beats: Solomon's message to Hiram explaining why now is the time to build, verses 1 to 6; Hiram's joyful reply and the treaty between the two kings, verses 7 to 12; and Solomon's labor force quarrying stone and preparing timber for the temple, verses 13 to 18.

units.label: Solomon's message to Hiram
units.note: rest at last, so now I will build

verses.text: Now when Hiram king of Tyre heard that Solomon had been anointed king in his father's place, he sent envoys to Solomon; for Hiram had always been a friend of David.
And Solomon relayed this message to Hiram:

“As you are well aware, due to the wars waged on all sides against my father David, he could not build a {{bayit|house}} for the {{shem|Name}} of the LORD his God until the LORD had put his enemies under his feet.
But now the LORD my God has given me {{menuchah|rest}} on every side, and there is no adversary or crisis.

So behold, I plan to build a house for the Name of the LORD my God, according to what the LORD said to my father David: ‘I will put your son on your throne in your place, and he will build the house for My Name.’

Now therefore, order that cedars of Lebanon be cut down for me. My servants will be with your servants, and I will pay your servants whatever wages you set, for you know that there are none among us as skilled in logging as the Sidonians.”

units.label: Hiram's reply and the treaty between kings
units.note: cedar and cypress for wheat and oil

verses.text: When Hiram received Solomon's message, he rejoiced greatly and said, “Blessed be the LORD this day! He has given David a wise son over this great people!”
Then Hiram sent a reply to Solomon, saying: “I have received your message; I will do all you desire regarding the cedar and cypress timber.

My servants will haul the logs from Lebanon to the Sea, and I will float them as rafts by sea to the place you specify. There I will separate the logs, and you can take them away. And in exchange, you can meet my needs by providing my household with food.”
So Hiram provided Solomon with all the cedar and cypress timber he wanted,
and year after year Solomon would provide Hiram with 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household, as well as 20,000 baths of pure olive oil.
And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as He had promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a {{berit|treaty}}.

units.label: Solomon's labor force
units.note: quarrying and preparing for the house of the LORD

verses.text: Then King Solomon conscripted a labor force of 30,000 men from all Israel.
He sent them to Lebanon in monthly shifts of 10,000 men, so that they would spend one month in Lebanon and two months at home. And Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor.
Solomon had 70,000 porters and 80,000 stonecutters in the mountains,
not including his 3,300 foremen who supervised the workers.
And the king commanded them to quarry large, costly stones to lay the foundation of the temple with dressed stones.
So Solomon's and Hiram's builders, along with the Gebalites, quarried the stone and prepared the timber and stone for the construction of the temple.

bayit.gloss: House, home, or temple. Solomon speaks repeatedly of building a bayit for the LORD, the same word used for an ordinary household, showing that the temple is conceived as God's dwelling place among His people rather than merely a national monument.

shem.gloss: Name. Solomon says the house is built for the Name of the LORD, not simply for the LORD directly, a Deuteronomic way of speaking, Deuteronomy 12:11, that ties the temple to God's revealed character and reputation dwelling among His people, rather than confining God Himself to a building.

menuchah.gloss: Rest, quietness from strife. David could not build because he lacked this rest, verse 3; Solomon can build precisely because the LORD has now given him menuchah on every side, verse 4, fulfilling God's word that David's son, a man of rest, would build the house, 1 Chronicles 22:9.

berit.gloss: Covenant or treaty. The BSB footnote notes that forms of this Hebrew word are elsewhere translated covenant in most passages. Hiram and Solomon's treaty of mutual provision uses the same vocabulary Scripture uses for God's covenants with His people, framing even this international agreement within the larger biblical language of binding, faithful relationship.

basic.context: As soon as Solomon's fame for wisdom spreads, Hiram king of Tyre, an old friend of David, reaches out to the new king. Solomon explains that his father could not build a house for the LORD's Name because of constant warfare, but the LORD has now given him rest on every side, so the time to build has finally come. Hiram gladly agrees to supply cedar and cypress timber in exchange for wheat and olive oil, the two kings make a treaty, and Solomon then conscripts a massive labor force, Israelites working in Lebanon on monthly rotation alongside porters and stonecutters, to quarry stone and prepare timber for the temple's foundation. The key questions this chapter raises are why rest from war was the necessary condition for building, what it means that God's house is built through partnership with a Gentile king, and how the enormous cost in labor and materials shapes our reading of what follows in chapter 6.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing genuine diplomatic and economic arrangements; it is not a manual for church building programs today. What the chapter teaches as enduring truth is that God's timing matters, rest precedes building, that God can use even a pagan king's resources and goodwill to advance His purposes, and that costly, careful preparation properly precedes any work done for the LORD.
basic.originalLanguages: Solomon speaks of building a bayit, a house, for the shem, the Name, of the LORD, a Deuteronomic phrase that ties the temple to God's presence and reputation among the nations rather than confining Him to a building. He can build now because the LORD has given him menuchah, rest, on every side, precisely the condition God had said would qualify David's son to build, 1 Chronicles 22:9. And the whole arrangement with Hiram is sealed by a berit, a treaty, the same word Scripture elsewhere reserves for covenant, its ordinary language now framing an alliance between an Israelite and a Gentile king.
basic.typology: Gentile resources, cedar from Lebanon, and Gentile labor from Tyre and Byblos, are gathered into the preparation of God's house, foreshadowing the day when the nations themselves would be gathered into the house of God, no longer merely supplying its materials but becoming living stones within it. Solomon's rest, given by the LORD as the condition for building, points to the greater rest Christ gives, in whom alone true temple building, the building of the church, can go forward.
basic.christ: Solomon can only build because the LORD has first given him rest on every side, verse 4, a rest promised beforehand as the mark of the son who would build God's house, 1 Chronicles 22:9-10. Jesus is the greater Son of David who both gives true rest, Matthew 11:28-29, and builds a greater house, His church, upon that finished rest, Matthew 16:18. And just as Gentile Hiram gladly supplies what Israel lacks so that the LORD's house can be built, the New Testament shows the nations themselves, once outsiders, being built together into a holy temple in the Lord, Ephesians 2:19-22.
basic.god: God is sovereign over international affairs, moving a foreign king to supply exactly what His temple requires, and faithful to His covenant word to David that a son of rest would build the house for His Name. He is also a God who values careful, costly, unhurried preparation, willing to spend years gathering timber, stone, and labor before the temple proper is even begun, showing that diligent preparation itself can be an act of worship.
basic.crossReferences: First Chronicles 22 records David's own preparations and the LORD's word that his son, a man of peace, would build the house. Second Samuel 7 contains the original promise that David's son would build a house for the LORD's Name. Ephesians 2 speaks of Jew and Gentile alike being built together into a holy temple in the Lord, and Matthew 11 speaks of the rest that Christ, the greater Son of David, gives His people.
basic.oneStory: David longed to build God a house but was a man of war; here his son, given rest by the LORD, gathers Gentile skill and Israelite labor to prepare for the task. This is one more step in the long story of God dwelling among His people, from the tabernacle in the wilderness toward the temple in Jerusalem, and ultimately toward Christ, the true temple, in whom God tabernacles among us and gathers people from every nation into one house built for His Name.

context.literary:
The chapter is built almost like embedded correspondence, Solomon's message quoted in full, verses 3 to 6, and Hiram's reply quoted in full, verses 8 and 9, bracketing the narrator's own brief connecting comments. This documentary style, letting the participants speak in their own words rather than only summarizing their agreement, gives the treaty an official, almost archival feel, the kind of record a royal scribe might have kept rather than a storyteller's paraphrase. The same technique reappears much later in Israel's history, when official correspondence is quoted at length in Ezra 4 through 6 to authenticate the postexilic temple's own difficult history.

The chapter also moves in a deliberate sequence from words to things. It opens with speech, an exchange of messages between two kings who have not yet met in person, moves through an agreement stated in exact quantities, cedar and cypress for so many measures of wheat and oil each year, and ends with raw labor, tens of thousands of named and unnamed workers quarrying stone in the mountains. The temple itself is still nowhere in view by the chapter's last verse; every sentence here is preparation, gathering the words, the materials, and the hands that the next chapter will finally put to use.
context.historical:
Tyre in Hiram's day was less a single city than an island fortress just off the Phoenician coast, backed by mainland suburbs and famous across the ancient world for seafaring, purple dye, and skilled woodworking drawn from the cedar forests inland. Cedar from Lebanon was prized well beyond Israel's borders; other ancient Near Eastern literature outside the Bible likewise treats those same forests as material fit for the greatest building projects of kings and temples, a reputation Solomon's request in verse 6 simply takes for granted rather than needing to argue for.

Floating logs down the coast as lashed rafts, verse 9, was the standard, practical method for moving heavy timber long distances by sea before Solomon's men then broke the rafts apart near the coastal point closest to Jerusalem and hauled the wood overland the rest of the way. The Gebalites of verse 18, skilled stonemasons from Byblos, came from a city whose name later gave the Greek language its word for book, since Byblos was for centuries a major port through which Egyptian papyrus reached the wider Mediterranean world, a small sign of how thoroughly this coastal region's trade networks touched cultures far beyond Israel and Phoenicia alike.

The specific quantities named, twenty thousand cors of wheat and olive oil yearly, verse 11, represent a substantial, ongoing national expense, not a single payment, showing that Israel's side of this bargain was a long-term commitment rather than a one-time gift.
context.canonical:
Second Chronicles retells this same negotiation with its own additional details, including Hiram's gift of a skilled craftsman, and situates it as the opening move of an even longer building account, 2 Chronicles 2:1-16. Reading Kings and Chronicles side by side shows two inspired historians choosing slightly different details from the same underlying history, one stressing the treaty's diplomacy, the other its craftsmanship.

This chapter's arrangement becomes a template rather than a one-time event. When the exiles return generations later to rebuild the ruined temple, they follow this exact precedent, paying Sidonians and Tyrians with food, drink, and oil to bring cedar from Lebanon by sea, Ezra 3:7, deliberately reenacting Solomon's original agreement as the recognized, proper way to secure material for the LORD's house.

The chapter's confident, cheerful tone also carries a cost that only appears many chapters later. Twenty years and a great deal of gold after this treaty is signed, Solomon must cede twenty towns in Galilee to Hiram to help settle the account, 1 Kings 9:10-14, and the labor force organized here under Adoniram becomes, by 1 Kings 12, the specific grievance that helps tear the kingdom in two. Nothing in chapter 5 is dishonest, but Kings, read to the end, lets the reader see what this chapter's optimism did not yet have to reckon with.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The chapter means to show that the temple's construction begins long before the first stone is set in place, in careful diplomacy, honest acknowledgment of God's timing, and costly, patient gathering of ordinary materials. The author wants the reader to see Solomon's initiative as itself an act of obedience, not a delay, since he moves the moment rest is given rather than waiting for some further sign, and to see Hiram's willing partnership as evidence that God's purposes for His house can draw in resources and goodwill from far beyond Israel's own borders without compromising what makes that house distinct.

The author is equally concerned to distinguish this partnership from the more dangerous alliances the book will describe elsewhere. Hiram supplies timber and labor for wages; he is never married into Solomon's household the way Pharaoh's daughter and other foreign wives will be, a distinction the narrator lets the reader notice without stating it outright.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a specific ancient treaty and a specific ancient labor conscription; it does not prescribe forced labor, a particular trade arrangement, or any specific method of construction for God's people today. Modern readers are not meant to reproduce corvee labor drafts or barter timber for grain.

What does endure is the underlying pattern, that building for the LORD properly begins with God-given rest rather than anxious striving, that wise use of whatever resources and relationships are available, even resources supplied by outsiders to the covenant, honors God rather than compromising the work, and that unglamorous, years-long preparation is itself a fitting form of worship rather than a delay before the real work starts.

debates.question: Is Solomon's economic partnership with Hiram a compromise of Israel's separateness, similar to the marriage alliances flagged elsewhere in these chapters, or a legitimate use of the nations' gifts?

views.label: Legitimate and different in kind from the marriage alliances
views.case: This is a trade and labor agreement, not a marriage or an act of shared worship, and Hiram's own words bless the LORD by name, verse 7, showing recognition of Israel's God rather than syncretism, in clear contrast to the marriage alliance with Pharaoh's daughter that opens the previous chapter.

views.label: A partnership that still carried real, hidden cost
views.case: The heavy reliance on Gentile skill and materials, plus the enormous multi-year debt of wheat and oil, plants the seeds of the very economic strain that later forces Solomon to cede twenty Galilean towns to Hiram, 1 Kings 9:10-14, a cost this chapter's cheerful tone does not foresee.

debates.bearing: The chapter itself presents the arrangement positively, sealed with peace and a treaty, verse 12, but Kings' later report of ceded towns shows the partnership was not without real, ongoing cost to Israel even though it was never a spiritual compromise.

debates.question: Are the 30,000 conscripted Israelites of verses 13 to 14 the same category of labor as the harsher forced labor 1 Kings 9:20-22 later imposes on non-Israelite peoples?

views.label: A distinct and more humane arrangement
views.case: Israelite laborers rotate one month away and two months at home, verse 14, unlike the more permanent forced labor later imposed only on Canaanite remnant peoples, 1 Kings 9:20-22, suggesting Solomon distinguished between citizen national service and harsher, conquered-people servitude.

views.label: A distinction that eroded with time
views.case: The later complaint about a heavy yoke, 1 Kings 12:4, seems to include Israelites broadly, and the very officer over this labor force, Adoniram, is later stoned by an Israelite crowd, 1 Kings 12:18, suggesting whatever distinction existed here did not hold indefinitely.

debates.bearing: This chapter's own numbers describe a rotation that reads as reasonable for its moment; later chapters let the reader watch whether that moderation held for the whole of Solomon's reign.

study.originalLanguages:
Solomon calls the Sidonians unmatched in logging, verse 6, literally hewers of trees, an old occupational phrase already used in Joshua's day for the lowest tier of temple labor imposed on the Gibeonites, hewers of wood and drawers of water, Joshua 9:21 and 27. It is a striking reversal that the very task once assigned to a conquered, servant people in Joshua's generation is here hired, respected, and paid for, from a free and prosperous Phoenician kingdom, at Israel's own request.

The 30,000 conscripted Israelites of verse 13 are gathered under a mas, a forced levy or corvee, the same category of labor Solomon later imposes, more harshly and permanently, on the remaining Canaanite peoples, 1 Kings 9:20-21. Applied here to Israelites themselves, though only in careful month-long rotations, the word already carries an edge Kings will let the reader feel more sharply once Rehoboam's officer over exactly this mas is stoned to death by an angry crowd, 1 Kings 12:18.

Solomon's stated purpose is to build a bayit, house, not for the LORD directly but for His shem, Name, verses 3 and 5, language rooted in Deuteronomy's own instruction that Israel would worship at the place the LORD your God will choose to make His Name dwell, Deuteronomy 12:11. The distinction matters theologically as much as grammatically; Solomon is not building a container for God Himself, an idea Solomon will state outright once the building is finished, will God indeed dwell on the earth, even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, 1 Kings 8:27, but a house bearing God's reputation and character among the nations.

Finally, the agreement itself is sealed as a berit, verse 12, the identical word Scripture uses for God's own covenants with Noah, Abraham, and David. Applying covenant vocabulary to an ordinary trade deal between two kings is not accidental; it signals that even this practical exchange of timber for wheat is described in the most serious relational terms Hebrew possesses, a bond, not merely a transaction.

The word shalom itself threads back to the previous chapter's celebration of a kingdom at peace on every side, and here it describes something more specific still, peace not merely within Israel's own borders but between two separate kings and two separate peoples, Israelite and Phoenician, sealed by treaty rather than by conquest. Throughout the negotiation both sides are called avadim, servants, Solomon's servants and Hiram's servants working side by side, verse 6, the same ordinary word Scripture uses for household workers and, elsewhere, for the LORD's own prophets, a shared vocabulary of service that places skilled Sidonian loggers and conscripted Israelites within a single sentence.

typology.type: Gentile skill, labor, and material gathered from Tyre and Byblos to build the house bearing the LORD's Name, verses 6, 18
typology.fulfillment: Centuries later the returning exiles rebuild the temple on the very same terms, paying the people of Sidon and Tyre with food, drink, and oil to bring cedar from Lebanon exactly as Solomon once did, Ezra 3:7, showing the pattern repeated rather than abandoned. Both scenes anticipate the New Testament's larger claim, that Gentiles once far off are built together into a dwelling place for God, Ephesians 2:13 and 22, no longer merely supplying materials for someone else's house but becoming living stones within it themselves, 1 Peter 2:5.

typology.type: Rest given by the LORD as the necessary precondition before building can begin, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: David could not build amid war; Solomon builds only once rest has already been granted, not earned by his own labor first. The order matters, rest comes before the work, not as its reward. Jesus offers precisely this order to weary souls, come to Me and I will give you rest, before ever calling them to take up His yoke and learn from Him, Matthew 11:28-29, and He goes on to build His own house, the church, entirely on a rest already secured by His finished work, Matthew 16:18.

typology.type: A treaty of peace, sealed in covenant language, between an Israelite king and a Gentile king who blesses the LORD's name, verses 7, 12
typology.fulfillment: Hiram is never absorbed into Israel, yet he genuinely praises Israel's God, an outsider recognizing what insiders already knew. That partial, real recognition anticipates a fuller one, the day when the kingdom of the world itself, not merely one sympathetic king, has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, Revelation 11:15, and every nation, not only Tyre's ruler, joins in blessing the God whose house they once only helped to supply.

study.christ:
Solomon is remembered in this chapter as the builder of the house, verse 18, yet Hebrews insists that whoever builds any house is honored less than the house itself, and that ultimately God is the builder of everything, Hebrews 3:3-4. Solomon supervises construction; he does not, in the end, originate the house's true purpose or its final glory, both of which belong to the God whose Name it bears. Christ stands in a different relation to His own house entirely, not merely commissioned to build it but, as the eternal Son, sharing in its very foundation, the builder of the house has more honor than the house itself, Hebrews 3:3, because the house He builds, the church, is raised on His own life laid down and taken up again.

That last detail matters. When Jesus is later asked for a sign, He answers, destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, and John explains, He was speaking about the temple of His body, John 2:19 and 21. Solomon prepared timber and stone for years before a single wall rose; Christ's own body was the temple destroyed and rebuilt in three days, a preparation and a completion neither Solomon's labor force nor Hiram's craftsmen could ever have imagined needing.

The chapter's quiet Gentile presence also deepens once read through Peter's later language. Hiram and his Sidonian workers supply timber but never enter the house they help to raise; Peter tells believers, Jew and Gentile alike, like living stones, you yourselves are being built into a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:5, no longer outside contributors to someone else's building project but actual, permanent stones inside the structure itself.

And where Solomon's labor force worked in monthly shifts for years merely to gather materials, verses 13 to 18, the writer to the Hebrews describes a rest that requires no further building at all, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9, the true and final version of the very rest that let Solomon begin his own, far smaller and far more temporary, work.
study.god:
God's ordinary means are on full display in this chapter. Nothing here is miraculous in the way earlier chapters of Israel's history sometimes are, no fire from heaven, no dividing of a sea. Instead, the temple's first real progress happens through payment for timber, wages for skilled labor, and years of quarrying stone, exactly the kind of unremarkable transaction that could happen between any two ancient kingdoms. Scripture does not treat this as a lesser mode of God's activity; the LORD who parts seas is equally, and just as truly, the LORD who moves a foreign king's willing heart to strike a fair trade deal for cedar and wheat.

God is also shown keeping a promise across a longer stretch of time than any single chapter can show. The word that David's son would build the house, first spoken through Nathan in 2 Samuel 7 and repeated to Solomon directly by David himself, 1 Chronicles 22:9-10, had to wait through the remainder of David's long reign, through wars, rebellions, and family grief, before circumstances finally matched what had been promised. God's faithfulness in this chapter is not sudden; it is the quiet arrival, at last, of something spoken decades earlier and simply waited for.

He is also shown honoring careful, deliberate order over haste. Verses 13 to 18 describe years of preparation, quarrying, hauling, dressing stone, before the temple's actual construction is even mentioned. A God who could have supplied a finished temple in an instant instead lets His people spend real years gathering what the task requires, teaching, by the shape of the story itself rather than by any stated command, that faithfulness to Him is not measured only by dramatic breakthroughs but by the patient accumulation of ordinary, costly obedience. Even the years spent negotiating wages and hauling stone belong, on this reading, to the worship the temple was built to house, not merely to the logistics that made worship possible afterward.

crossReferences.note: The LORD's original promise to David, that his own offspring would build a house for His Name and that his throne would be established forever, is the word Solomon explicitly cites in verse 5 as his authority to build now. This chapter is the promise's first concrete step toward being kept.

David tells Solomon directly that he could not build because of his wars and bloodshed, but that a son of rest would build the house instead. This chapter shows that very word coming true almost immediately once David is gone and rest has been given.

Moses had told Israel that once settled in the land they would bring their offerings to the place the LORD your God will choose to make His Name dwell. Solomon's repeated phrase, a house for the Name, verses 3 and 5, deliberately picks up this old, still-unfulfilled instruction from the wilderness generation.

The Gibeonites, having tricked Israel into a covenant, are sentenced to be perpetual hewers of wood and drawers of water for the altar of the LORD. Solomon's request for skilled loggers, verse 6, uses the identical occupational language for work now performed by a free, paid, allied kingdom rather than a subjugated one.

Generations later, exiles rebuilding the ruined temple pay the Sidonians and Tyrians with food, drink, and oil to bring cedar from Lebanon by sea, in language that echoes this chapter almost point for point. Solomon's original arrangement with Hiram becomes the template the returning remnant consciously follows to rebuild what Babylon destroyed.

Once the temple stands, Solomon himself asks whether God can truly dwell on earth at all, since even the highest heaven cannot contain Him. The house prepared for so painstakingly in this chapter was never meant to hold God, only to bear His Name among a watching world.

Twenty years after this treaty, Solomon must give Hiram twenty towns in Galilee to help cover the cost of all the cedar, cypress, and gold Hiram had supplied. The cheerful, mutually agreeable exchange of this chapter turns out to carry a long-term price its own optimistic tone does not anticipate.

When Rehoboam refuses to lighten his father's demands, the northern tribes rebel outright, and the very officer in charge of the forced labor, the same office held here by Adoniram, is stoned to death by the crowd. The labor force organized so matter-of-factly in this chapter becomes, one generation later, the specific grievance that splits the kingdom.

Jesus invites the weary to come to Him for rest before He ever asks them to take up His yoke and learn from Him. Solomon could only begin building once the LORD had already granted him rest; Christ offers a yoke that is, He says, easy and light, unlike the heavy yoke Solomon's own labor policy would later become.

Paul tells Gentile believers they are no longer strangers but fellow citizens, built together into a dwelling place for God. Hiram's cedar and Gebalite stonemasons supplied materials for a house they themselves could never enter; the New Testament describes Gentiles no longer merely supplying the building but being built into it themselves.

study.oneStory:
When Israel first built a place for God to dwell among them, the tabernacle in the wilderness, God filled specific Israelite craftsmen, Bezalel and Oholiab, with His own Spirit for the work, to devise artistic designs in every craft, Exodus 35:30-35. The circle of skilled hands was drawn narrowly, from within Israel alone. By the time Solomon prepares to build a permanent house two hundred years later, that circle has already begun to widen, Sidonian loggers, Gebalite stonemasons, and Solomon's own conscripted Israelites all working side by side on the same project, still for the LORD's Name, but no longer through Israelite hands only.

This widening does not stop with the temple's stones. Centuries later Gentile magi travel to worship the newborn king of the Jews, Matthew 2:1-11, and after the resurrection the gospel itself moves outward to Gentile cities with the same energy that once moved cedar logs down the coast from Lebanon. What begins in this chapter as hired labor for a building becomes, by the New Testament, an invitation into the family the building was always meant to serve.

The story's final destination makes the earlier chapters, tabernacle, temple, treaty with Hiram, look like careful preparation for something none of them could finish. John's vision of the new creation contains no temple at all, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22, because the dwelling itself is no longer a building but a Person, present directly among a people gathered from every nation Hiram's kingdom once merely represented. The years of quarrying and hauling timber recorded in this chapter were never really about a building; they were preparation for a presence that a house of cedar and stone could only ever borrow for a season.

quiz.q: Why, according to Solomon's message in verses 3 to 4, could David not build the house but Solomon now can?

options.text: David faced constant wars on every side, but the LORD has now given Solomon rest on every side, with no adversary or crisis.
options.note: This is the reason Solomon himself states plainly in verses 3-4.

options.text: David was simply too old to undertake such a large building project.
options.note: Age is not the stated reason; the text explicitly names David's wars as the obstacle.

options.text: David did not have enough wealth to fund the temple.
options.note: Wealth is not mentioned as the barrier; the stated reason is the absence of rest from war.

options.text: There was no reason given for the delay; it was simply Solomon's personal preference to build now.
options.note: Solomon gives a clear, specific reason rooted in God's gift of rest, not personal preference.

quiz.q: How does Hiram respond to Solomon's message, and what does his response reveal, verse 7?

options.text: He rejoices greatly and blesses the LORD for giving David a wise son, recognizing God's hand in Solomon's reign even as a foreign king.
options.note: Verse 7 records Hiram's explicit praise of the LORD, an unusual acknowledgment from a Gentile ruler.

options.text: He is mainly interested in the trade benefits of wheat and oil promised in return.
options.note: The exchange of goods is real and follows in verses 8-11, but Hiram's own words in verse 7 focus on blessing the LORD, not the trade terms.

options.text: He refuses at first and must be persuaded through further negotiation.
options.note: The text shows Hiram responding with immediate joy, not initial refusal.

options.text: He shows no reaction at all to Solomon's request.
options.note: Verse 7 explicitly describes Hiram's joyful, worshipful reaction.

quiz.q: What did the exchange between Hiram and Solomon actually involve, verses 8 to 11?

options.text: Hiram supplied cedar and cypress timber floated by sea from Lebanon, and Solomon supplied wheat and olive oil as food for Hiram's household.
options.note: Verses 8-11 detail exactly this mutual exchange of timber for agricultural provisions.

options.text: Hiram supplied only labor, while Solomon paid entirely in silver and gold.
options.note: Silver and gold are not mentioned here; the stated exchange is timber for wheat and oil, plus Israelite labor alongside Hiram's servants.

options.text: Solomon supplied all the timber while Hiram supplied only food.
options.note: The arrangement is reversed from this; Hiram supplied the timber, and Solomon supplied the food.

options.text: There was no real exchange; Hiram simply gave the timber as a free gift.
options.note: The text describes a mutual arrangement, an exchange of goods, not a one-sided gift.

quiz.q: What does the scale of Solomon's labor force, 30,000 conscripted Israelites in rotating shifts plus 150,000 porters and stonecutters, verses 13 to 16, suggest about the temple's preparation?

options.text: Building God's house was a massive, costly, nationwide undertaking, requiring careful and patient preparation long before construction itself began.
options.note: The detailed numbers underscore the scale and seriousness of the preparation described in this chapter.

options.text: It shows only that Solomon enjoyed displaying his personal power through large numbers.
options.note: The numbers are large, but the chapter frames them around preparing the LORD's house, not personal display.

options.text: It shows that the temple was actually a small, modest structure requiring little labor.
options.note: The described labor force is enormous, indicating a major building project, not a modest one.

options.text: It shows that Solomon relied entirely on Hiram's workers and used no Israelite labor.
options.note: Verse 13 explicitly says Solomon conscripted 30,000 men from all Israel.

quiz.q: What is the significance of verse 12, where the LORD gives Solomon wisdom and peace results between Hiram and Solomon, sealed by a treaty?

options.text: It shows God's promised wisdom producing tangible peace and a binding, covenant-like partnership between an Israelite king and a Gentile king.
options.note: The verse directly links God's gift of wisdom to the peaceable treaty that follows, using covenant language, berit, for the agreement.

options.text: It shows that Solomon and Hiram were already close personal friends with no formal agreement needed.
options.note: Hiram was a friend of David, verse 1, but verse 12 specifically describes a formal treaty, not merely informal friendship.

options.text: It shows that the peace between the two kings was temporary and quickly broken.
options.note: The text presents this peace and treaty positively, with no indication in this chapter that it was short-lived.

options.text: It shows that God's wisdom had nothing to do with Solomon's foreign relations.
options.note: The verse explicitly ties God's gift of wisdom to the resulting peace and treaty.

questions: Solomon could only build because the LORD had first given him rest. Where in your life is God asking you to wait for His rest before taking on a new work, rather than forcing it in your own strength?

Hiram, an outsider to Israel's covenant, rejoiced and blessed the LORD when he heard of Solomon's wisdom. Who in your life might see God's hand in you before you expect it, and how can you make that testimony clear?

Building the temple required years of unseen preparation, quarrying stone and gathering timber, before a single wall went up. What patient, unglamorous preparation is God calling you to right now for something you cannot yet see completed?

The treaty between Hiram and Solomon shows God weaving even ordinary trade and diplomacy into His larger purposes. Where do you need to trust that God is at work in your everyday commitments and partnerships, not only in dramatic moments?
This whole chapter exists to prepare a house for the Name of the LORD. What are you preparing your heart or your household for this season, and is it ultimately built for God's name or your own?

translationNotes.note: 'The Sea' in the BSB footnote refers to the Mediterranean Sea, also called the Great Sea, the route by which Hiram's servants floated the cedar and cypress rafts south from Lebanon.

The BSB footnote follows the LXX reading, supported by 2 Chronicles 2:10, of 20,000 baths of pure olive oil; the Hebrew text reads twenty cors of pure or pressed oil, a notable textual variant in quantity.

The BSB footnote observes that forms of the Hebrew berit, translated 'treaty' here, are rendered 'covenant' in most other passages, tying this diplomatic agreement to the same vocabulary Scripture uses for God's covenants with His people.
